title: Generic large-publication and static-search design
status: Research recommendation; reference-only prototypes, not production integration or release qualification
recommendation_markdown:
# Recommendation

Make large publications practical through **generic source streaming, literal metadata facets, normalized search storage, and lazy index delivery**. Keep software releases, contract-element identity, compatibility rules, and release applicability in the producer repository. Riverhog is a useful demanding workload, not a new GuavaJam document type.

The earlier four-improvement sketch was intent calibration. This investigation changes two important parts of that sketch: deduplicate stored source text without silently deduplicating occurrence-level FTS postings, and distinguish independently ranked database shards from physical chunks of one logical database. Query execution and oversized-passage evidence are additional high-impact improvements.

This is a research-backed design and implementation handoff. The reference branch contains reproducible experiments and evidence; it is not an integration branch and does not qualify a release.

## Why this is needed

At GuavaJam [`54fce07b619628a5e92be946be4b189873ddf1a0`](https://github.com/nashspence/guavajam/tree/54fce07b619628a5e92be946be4b189873ddf1a0), supporting-document validation/rendering imposes 128-document and 100-MiB aggregate limits. Snapshotting, generated inventories, search building, and browser loading have other independent bounds. Removing only the first limits leaves both failures and whole-corpus memory retention elsewhere.

Current work search also downloads an all-editions database to serve an ordinary Documents query, although that view searches only titles and abstracts. Full-text passage/version/collection SQL materializes scores and six snippets for every matching occurrence; Documents does the corresponding work for two fields. Counting and paging repeat that work. The existing gzip loader already streams decoding into WASM; it nevertheless needs the entire decoded database resident.

Source boundaries remain unchanged: GuavaJam owns source validity/publication authority; the optional static generator owns rendering, indexes, query planning, delivery, caching, and UI. Search derivatives do not become publication authority.

## Evidence and experimental scope

**Real corpus:** Riverhog [`be483fd6d567616d5fcd355202d61f1e682efe75`](https://github.com/nashspence/riverhog/tree/be483fd6d567616d5fcd355202d61f1e682efe75) was cleanly regenerated through its maintained contract-candidate command, using its pinned Python 3.12.3/uv 0.11.24 and locked dependencies. It contains **5,947 contract elements**, 24 interface categories, and 100 authority labels. This replaces the earlier 4,258-definition proxy. The complete native reference supplies 30,116 heading-based chunks; the largest 100 documents contain approximately 55% of all native text.

A deterministic adapter then produced 5,947 supporting GFM files, all accepted by GuavaJam's unmodified per-file loader with Python 3.12.12/Pandoc 3.12.1. Every native text chunk roundtripped. Production navigation yields **36,063 passages**, including the visible metadata introductions, and 14,117,137 document-text bytes. The largest passage is 1,027,923 bytes. The adapter uses literal paragraphs to retain text; a final table/list/link/heading design must be qualified separately. On two sample documents, H2-plus-body markup nearly doubles passage-index text through section and block occurrences. These are not signed publications or the final Riverhog documentation site.

Five-edition history is deterministic modeled change, not observed software-release history: each subsequent edition changes 297 seeded documents and changes the literal `Example version` metadata on every document. Initial source hashes match the generated GFM bytes, and subsequent hashes are computed from the actual serialized modeled GFM. The searchable fields, occurrence IDs, and parsed citations are compared between layout candidates. Modeled Git revisions and citation URLs are fixture context, not claims about real published editions.

| Layout | One edition raw | One edition gzip | Five editions raw | Five editions gzip |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Current schema baseline | 130.33 | 11.90 | 645.91 | 47.08 |
| Normalized text/citations | 65.42 | 10.85 | 259.04 | 32.48 |
| Shared ordered body segments | 49.83 | 9.20 | 180.90 | 24.13 |
| Documents directory only | 4.44 | 1.13 | 16.86 | 4.37 |

All sizes use MiB and deterministic gzip level 9. The baseline uses the current work-index SQL schema with the same added facet relations; it is not a complete signed-site build. The compact variant normalizes shared text, edition facts, and citation presentation while retaining each original FTS occurrence. The segmented variant additionally reconstructs exact document text from separately shared ordered segments. The directory variant retains only the complete Documents-search corpus and required metadata, not passage or version-search capability. Its router/manifest integration remains to implement.

Under the controlled browser profile, the one-edition Documents directory loaded in **1.70 seconds cold / 0.112 seconds warm**, transferring 1.13 MiB cold and no index bytes warm. The full segmented index needed **8.56 seconds cold / 8.02 seconds warm** in the isolated repeat and transferred 9.20 MiB on both loads in that test context. Runtime assets added approximately 0.56 MiB cold. Earlier overlapping runs were slower and are retained, not discarded.

There are three distinct correctness checks: exhaustive original source/navigation/metadata fidelity; **38 native query cases for each of three layouts**, including count, ordering, score, excerpt and parsed-citation parity; and **15 complete unchanged-production-worker messages per layout** in Chromium, including anchor targeting and display highlights. The five-edition fixture also passed full layout integrity/content checks and browser transport-query parity, but not the complete current-edition query matrix.

On the loaded current-edition index, a broad passage query took a median **1,590 ms with the current query plan versus 303 ms with late evidence generation**, over three warm iterations in the isolated run. A separate large-body evidence-window prototype reduced the body-excerpt generation after selecting the winning result from **563.5 to 7.6 ms** for a passage case and **701.3 to 3.3 ms** for a document/version case, while preserving primary matching, ranking, anchors and citations. The chosen excerpt intentionally changes but remains highlighted, exact-source evidence. These are specific-case observations, not workload-wide latency guarantees.

The pinned SQLite WASM is 3.54.1-build1. The actual browser is Chromium 158.0.8127.88 through Playwright 1.64.1; its bundled Chromium download was unavailable, so that browser pin was not exercised. Node was 24.22.3 rather than the repository's 24.10.0. WASM heap and explicit cache measurements are not total browser-process peak memory.

Other decisive findings:

- Removing only aggregate source guards lets pinned validation accept 4,000 valid documents and a separate 105-MiB supporting corpus. Invalid anchor, metadata, link, symlink, and individual-size cases retain their rejection behavior. Streaming batch Git extraction was byte/order equivalent: 16,000 tiny files took about 3.6 seconds versus 96.3 seconds for the stock path, with lower measured Python RSS. These are single-run extraction/validation observations, not full rendering throughput.
- The actual cache writer/reader rejects a synthetic 4,000-document rendered-file inventory using production filenames: its `CACHE.json` is 1,232,256 bytes, exceeding the separate 1-MiB ceiling. This was not a full 4,000-document render. Renderer, validator, and NAV/VIEW/SITE inventories also retain whole-corpus structures. Aggregate-limit removal alone is not a scalable build.
- Native and WASM tests show that counting membership separately, selecting the winning/page IDs, and obtaining evidence only for visible rows preserves query results while removing substantial work. Deterministic counterexamples show that deduplicating FTS rows or merging shard-local BM25 scores changes ranking. Mixed body/author/provenance terms must still match within one exact occurrence.
- Exact metadata facets work with low-cardinality Interface, medium-cardinality Authority, and 5,947 distinct Element IDs. A covering membership index is dramatically faster for selective identifiers than repeated JSON scans, but the best join plan varies with text/facet selectivity. Option enumeration needs bounded pages; do not eagerly ship every distinct value to a dropdown.
- Fifty-edition **text-payload** sensitivity is separate from measured database size. Repeated edits to the largest 297 documents create far more unique document text than random 297-document edits. A changed visible version field makes almost every whole-document string unique: stable body segments must be shareable independently of metadata. These calculations are not FTS, compression, or browser estimates.

## Proposed design

### 1. Separate valid publication size from operational resource budgets

Remove the arbitrary total supporting-document count and aggregate byte policy once the following paths can process larger inputs safely. Batch Git enumeration/blob reads, stream each blob to bounded storage, and maintain explicit framing, path/type, truncation, deadline, and child-process cleanup checks. Keep protective per-operation limits (including the tested 8-MiB source-item and 20-MiB snapshot-blob guards) or expose deliberate trusted-operator budgets with precise errors; do not interpret a reader/build budget as a software-version or publication rule.

Replace whole-corpus AST retention for link checking with a compact on-disk inventory of documents, anchors, and outgoing references. Write rendered outputs incrementally. Evolve generator-owned NAV, VIEW, CACHE, SITE, and search inventories coherently; streaming or hierarchical inventories must preserve exact source identities and complete file coverage. Change core publication catalogs only if measured necessity and compatibility evidence require it. Do not simply raise every JSON limit. Cache invalidation/recovery and atomic publication must continue to work when a build fails halfway through.

### 2. Add generic exact metadata filtering

Carry the existing supporting metadata mapping into verified source-derived navigation and index records. Store literal values in normalized relations with covering indexes. A document occurrence owns its memberships; passages inherit them through that occurrence.

Specify OR within selected values for one key and AND across different keys. Preserve Unicode, case, numeric-looking strings, display order, and missing/empty distinctions; an empty list has no value membership. Bind labels/values as SQL parameters. Add bounded, searchable, deterministically ordered facet-option pages and persist filter state in URLs. Text-match eligibility, facet totals, count, pagination, and visible results must describe the same selected scope.

No special `riverhog_version`, semantic-version parsing, contract equivalence, release intervals, or inferred applicability belongs in GuavaJam or the generator.

### 3. Normalize stored content while retaining occurrence semantics

Keep shared ordered source-text segments and structural passage information separate from document/edition occurrences. Occurrences bind repository/work, revision, exact source digest, path, anchor, scope, order, and citation context. Store repeated edition and citation display facts once and reconstruct presentation for returned rows.

Use FTS5 external-content tables/views to reconstruct the exact searchable fields, keeping the existing tokenizer, positions, document sizes, and occurrence-level postings. The current six fields include edition-specific author, abstract, labels, and Git facts. A content hash is an internal optimization key, not a citation identity. Verify external-content consistency with the FTS integrity command as well as relational integrity.

Capture ordered source blocks while extracting navigation. **Do not reconstruct arbitrary document text by concatenating overlapping section/passage records.** The experimental flat adapter permits that equation and asserts it; a general implementation must retain exact separators, interstitial text, quotation scopes, and overlapping source ranges explicitly.

### 4. Bound query and visible-evidence work

Compile active constraints into indexed membership queries. Count matching entities without generating snippets. Select winning records and the requested page with the required deterministic tie-breaks; calculate relevance only where the requested ordering/grouping needs it. Fetch visible excerpts/citation presentation for those selected occurrence IDs, preserving mixed-field matches and exact-source evidence.

For large text bodies, maintain a separate bounded evidence-window index or equivalent position-aware source excerpt structure. It helps select a readable highlighted excerpt; it must not determine full-text membership, result ranking, or citation identity. Main full-occurrence FTS still handles terms that span evidence windows. Keep exact source offsets/bytes, bounded overlap, safe token boundaries, and an explicit correct fallback for an oversized unbroken token. The preferred excerpt may change, but every displayed text result must retain genuine highlighted evidence from its winning source occurrence.

### 5. Make delivery reflect the query scope, and preserve a complete history path

Publish a small immutable search manifest and a separately downloadable Documents index. Lazy-load full-text data only for the requested work/edition/document/search surface. Current/selected-edition indexes are generic GuavaJam scopes; software-release interpretation stays outside them. The ranking corpus is a declared logical scope, independent of chunk/cache layout; an ordinary facet selection need not redefine that corpus. If selected-edition indexing changes the ranking scope, declare and test that semantic choice explicitly.

For large **all-history** search, the recommended next transport is **content-addressed compressed physical chunks of one logical SQLite database**, with bounded decoded and compressed caches. This retains a single global FTS corpus, matching/counting semantics, and global relevance. Use measured byte budgets, not a fixed number of hash-prefix shards. A 1-MiB decoded chunk and a 32-MiB decoded cache are useful starting experiments, not source-format constants.

The browser prototype reads immutable **ordinary GET gzip objects**, with zero Range requests and no SQL server. It uses 1-MiB decoded chunks, a 32-MiB decoded LRU, an 8-MiB compressed LRU and an 8-MiB SQLite page-cache setting. All original 12 local/controlled cases and all three isolated-repeat cases matched the native baseline oracle for counts, result order, scores, excerpts and parsed citations.

| Controlled cold query | SQLite bytes transferred | Chunk requests | Request to result |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| One edition, broad `contract` | 3.35 MiB | 22 | 5.58 s |
| One edition, selective `transaction` | 2.74 MiB | 18 | 4.11 s |
| One edition, absent term | 1.22 MiB | 6 | 2.16 s |
| Five editions, broad `contract` | 11.25 MiB | 72 | 17.64 s |
| Five editions, selective `transaction` | 8.59 MiB | 55 | 14.39 s |
| Five editions, absent term | 1.24 MiB | 6 | 2.10 s |

One-edition rows use the isolated repeat; original observations were 5.74, 13.85 and 2.31 seconds respectively, with the selective observation affected by overlapping shared-host work. Five-edition rows are single-run observations. Network columns count SQLite chunks only; runtime and manifest bytes are separately recorded. This is a feasibility comparison, not a p95 benchmark or a claim that every query fetches a fixed fraction of the corpus.

The five-edition broad query transfers less than half the 24.13-MiB whole gzip, but still performs 251 inflations totaling 250.71 MiB of repeated decoded output. It takes 17.64 seconds in this profile, so archive latency and cache/decompression costs remain material. The measured decoded and compressed cache peaks stay within their declared limits; WASM heap for this case was 20.06 MiB, separately from those caches and browser/transient allocations.

Raw HTTP Range also worked, but with a strong ETag the earlier native-heading fixture's broad query still fetched 14.73 MiB in 93 requests and took 19.06 seconds, exceeding that fixture's 10.05-MiB whole gzip. Without the validator it was much worse. Raw Range is therefore not the default recommendation. The tested third-party VFS registration scaffold required an explicitly recorded compatibility adapter for the current WASM API. The compressed-chunk prototype validates lengths but does **not yet verify hashes in the worker** or provide production cancellation/corruption/recovery behavior.

Require a published manifest to bind schema/generation identity, logical database size/page size, chunk order, exact encoded/decoded lengths, and cryptographic hashes. Bound concurrent fetch/decode work, decoded-cache bytes, compressed-cache bytes, SQLite page/temporary memory, and outstanding queries independently. Preserve immutable cache reuse, explicit retry, cancellation, and visible complete/incomplete status. Unsupported or failed historical data must not silently yield a supposedly complete count or empty result.

**Decision gate:** do not ship a new VFS from storage projections alone. Qualify it with real browsers and the workload below, against whole gzip. If it cannot meet the required correctness/resource/maintenance budget, explicitly decide whether historical discovery becomes work/edition groups with relevance local to each group. That alternative must keep every historical match reachable with truthful progress/counts; it is a product-contract change, not a transparent global-ranking optimization. Do not silently substitute it or add Riverhog-specific behavior. The fast current-scope path alone does not close the large-history part of this issue.

## Riverhog producer responsibilities

Prefer stable supporting paths per contract element and complete immutable documentation-edition snapshots, with a clean hand-written manuscript. Riverhog owns a software-release → documentation-edition mapping, or emits explicit literal applicability memberships if it keeps a change-only page archive. “Changed in X” cannot tell a generic equality filter whether an unchanged element applies to Y, or whether it was removed.

Riverhog's independent documentation authoring history, frozen release documentation, native CLI help/OpenAPI/Python/distribution/OCI obligations, and contract-reference authority are separate producer policies. A site migration must preserve or intentionally redesign them in Riverhog; this issue does not transfer those responsibilities to GuavaJam. The inspected release-documentation commit [`9fb4a7d52b12a61e582be5656471979e8ee5e1e4`](https://github.com/nashspence/riverhog/tree/9fb4a7d52b12a61e582be5656471979e8ee5e1e4) has no populated authored manual to benchmark.

## Implementation sequence and acceptance

1. Land independent query/count/evidence improvements and exact metadata facets with current behavior or explicit reviewed semantics. Include a corpus/latency benchmark that does not depend on Riverhog at runtime.
2. Land normalized occurrence-preserving storage and an index-format migration/cache invalidation path. Prove six-field membership, ranking within each declared scope, stable ordering, excerpts, anchors, source hashes, and citations across metadata-only edits, changed/moved/removed/readded documents, duplicate bodies, Unicode, missing values, and deep large-body matches.
3. Land source/build streaming and inventory evolution, then remove aggregate corpus guards. Build the complete chosen supporting-GFM representation through signed-source validation, rendering, cache reuse, catalogs, directories, search, and atomic updates. Exercise malformed/oversized individual resources and interrupted builds.
4. Land the small directory/manifest routing path. Measure useful first interaction, cold/warm transfer, decoded bytes, peak WASM/JS/process memory as distinct quantities, query time, cancellation, and pagination. Do not assume a browser retains every large immutable response.
5. Qualify and select the all-history transport/policy. Include 1, 5, and 50 modeled editions, sparse and high-churn/skewed edits, large passages, common/rare/negative/mixed-field queries, exact facets, count and deep pagination. Exercise normal and constrained memory/network profiles, Chrome/Firefox/WebKit and representative mobile conditions, cache eviction, corruption, missing/truncated chunks, wrong generations, retry, and cancellation. Keep no-JavaScript static navigation functional.

Agree explicit performance budgets per scope before treating a measurement as a release gate. A reasonable first target to evaluate is a roughly 2-MiB ordinary directory-index transfer, with runtime assets and full-content/archive costs reported separately, plus bounded active memory. The controlled HTTP experiment delays each response by 40 ms and caps each response at nominal 10 Mbit/s; it is not a shared-bandwidth mobile network simulation. This investigation measured feasibility and identified failure modes; it does not establish cross-device p95 guarantees.
record_location: The owning issue carries the immutable publication record; no consumer disposition is asserted.
interpretation: Actual contract text and production-parsed navigation; modeled edition history, metadata facets and publication context.
Baseline SQL schema matches the source pin; this is not a full signed-source build.
First-edition source hashes match generated GFM; later fixture hashes are of actual serialized modeled GFM.
Retained original and isolated-repeat measurements expose contention; no cross-device p95 guarantee.
Indexes are reproducible outputs, not retained binary payloads. Retained corpus is sufficient for core index reproduction.
All-history chunking has browser feasibility proof but is gated on integrity, cancellation, recovery, cross-browser/mobile, larger-history and process-memory qualification.
